specStatements.text: The elements in the periodic table are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number and so that elements with similar properties are in columns, known as groups. The table is called a periodic table because similar properties occur at regular intervals.
Elements in the same group in the periodic table have the same number of electrons in their outer shell (outer electrons) and this gives them similar chemical properties.
Students should be able to:
explain how the position of an element in the periodic table is related to the arrangement of electrons in its atoms and hence to its atomic number
predict possible reactions and probable reactivity of elements from their positions in the periodic table.
Before the discovery of protons, neutrons and electrons, scientists attempted to classify the elements by arranging them in order of their atomic weights.
The early periodic tables were incomplete and some elements were placed in inappropriate groups if the strict order of atomic weights was followed.
Mendeleev overcame some of the problems by leaving gaps for elements that he thought had not been discovered and in some places changed the order based on atomic weights.
Elements with properties predicted by Mendeleev were discovered and filled the gaps. Knowledge of isotopes made it possible to explain why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct.
Students should be able to describe these steps in the development of the periodic table.
Elements that react to form positive ions are metals.
Elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.
The majority of elements are metals. Metals are found to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table. Non-metals are found towards the right and top of the periodic table.
Students should be able to:

explain the differences between metals and non-metals on the basis of their characteristic physical and chemical properties. This links to Group 0 , Group 1 , Group 7 and Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
explain how the atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to their position in the periodic table
explain how the reactions of elements are related to the arrangement of electrons in their atoms and hence to their atomic number.

The elements in Group 0 of the periodic table are called the noble gases. They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons. The noble gases have eight electrons in their outer shell, except for helium, which has only two electrons.
The boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass (going down the group).
Students should be able to:
explain how properties of the elements in Group 0 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms
predict properties from given trends down the group.
The elements in Group 1 of the periodic table are known as the alkali metals and have characteristic properties because of the single electron in their outer shell.
Students should be able to describe the reactions of the first three alkali metals with oxygen, chlorine and water.
In Group 1, the reactivity of the elements increases going down the group.
Students should be able to:
explain how properties of the elements in Group 1 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms
predict properties from given trends down the group.

The elements in Group 7 of the periodic table are known as the halogens and have similar reactions because they all have seven electrons in their outer shell. The halogens are non-metals and consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms.
Students should be able to describe the nature of the compounds formed when chlorine, bromine and iodine react with metals and non-metals.
In Group 7, the further down the group an element is the higher its relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point.
In Group 7, the reactivity of the elements decreases going down the group.
A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
Students should be able to:
explain how properties of the elements in Group 7 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms
predict properties from given trends down the group.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to: (lead-in to the two bullets that follow)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This line introduces the assessable bullets S04 and S05 and carries no content of its own. It is honoured by assessing exactly those two skills and nothing beyond them: q05 places an element from its electronic structure and q06 predicts reactivity from position. No question treats the lead-in as a separate piece of recall.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to: (lead-in to the three bullets that follow)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Honoured by assessing only the three bullets it introduces (S15, S16, S17): metal versus non-metal properties in q14, atomic structure and position in q15, and reactions traced back to electron arrangement in q16.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to: (lead-in to the two Group 0 bullets)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Honoured by assessing only S21, properties explained by the outer shell in q17 and q18, and S22, prediction from a given trend in q20.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to: (lead-in to the two Group 1 bullets)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Honoured by assessing only S27, the outer-shell explanation of the reactivity trend in q25, and S28, prediction from a given trend in q26.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to: (lead-in to the two Group 7 bullets)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Honoured by assessing only S35, the outer-shell explanation in q31, and S36, prediction from a given trend in q30. The separate displacement statement S33 is assessed by q32.

scopeNotes.statement: The reactions required are those of the first three alkali metals with oxygen, chlorine and water.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Questions on Group 1 reactions use only lithium, sodium and potassium, and only with water (q22), oxygen (q23) and chlorine (q24). Rubidium and caesium appear solely as prediction targets in q06 and q26, where the specification asks for prediction from trends rather than recall of their reactions.

scopeNotes.statement: The compounds required are those formed when chlorine, bromine and iodine react with metals and non-metals.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: q28 and q29 use chlorine only, once with a metal and once with a non-metal; q32 uses chlorine and bromine. Fluorine is never used, and astatine appears only as a prediction target in q30.

scopeNotes.statement: Prediction of properties is from given trends down the group; recall of particular data values is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: q20 and q30 supply the measured values inside the stem and ask only for a prediction from the pattern in them. No question requires a student to recall a boiling point or melting point figure.

concepts.definition: The arrangement of all the elements in order of atomic (proton) number, set out so that elements with similar properties fall in the same column.
A column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons and therefore similar chemical properties.
A row of the periodic table. The period number matches the number of occupied electron shells in an atom of the element.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It is the quantity that fixes an element's place in the modern periodic table.
The electrons in the highest occupied shell of an atom. They control how an element reacts, so elements sharing an outer-electron count behave alike.
The reappearance of similar properties at regular intervals along the order of the elements, which is why the table is called periodic.
The arrangement of an atom's electrons in shells, written as a list such as 2,8,7. The number of shells gives the period and the outer number gives the group.
The mass-based quantity used to order the elements before protons, neutrons and electrons had been discovered.
Empty places Mendeleev left in his table for elements he thought had not yet been discovered, so that the elements already known fell into suitable groups.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Their proportions set an element's atomic weight, which is why weight order is not always the correct order.
An element that reacts to form positive ions. Metals are the majority of the elements and are found to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table.
An element that does not form positive ions. Non-metals are found towards the right and top of the periodic table.
A particle formed when an atom loses one or more electrons, leaving more protons than electrons and so an overall positive charge.
The elements of Group 0. They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons.
An outer shell holding eight electrons, or two in the case of helium, so that the atom has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.
The boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass, that is, going down the group.
The elements of Group 1. They have characteristic properties because of the single electron in their outer shell.
An alkali metal reacts with water to give a metal hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas, for example 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2.
An alkali metal burns in oxygen to give a white metal oxide, for example 4Li + O2 → 2Li2O.
An alkali metal burns in chlorine to give a white metal chloride, for example 2K + Cl2 → 2KCl.
Reactivity increases going down Group 1, because the single outer electron is further from the nucleus and so is lost more easily.
The non-metal elements of Group 7. They have seven outer electrons, react in similar ways, and consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms.
The ionic salt formed when a halogen reacts with a metal, for example sodium chloride from sodium and chlorine.
The molecular compound formed when a halogen reacts with a non-metal, for example hydrogen chloride from hydrogen and chlorine.
Going down Group 7, the relative molecular mass, the melting point and the boiling point of the elements all increase.
Reactivity decreases going down Group 7, because the outer shell is further from the nucleus so an electron is attracted less strongly.
A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt, for example Cl2 + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br2.
As shells are added down a group the outer electrons sit further from the nucleus with more inner shells in between, so the nucleus holds them less strongly.

misconceptions.question: Does the group number tell you how many electron shells an atom has?
misconceptions.correct: The group number gives the number of outer electrons; the number of occupied shells gives the period.
misconceptions.misconception: The group number counts the shells, so 2,8,7 must be in Group 3 for its three shells.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both group and period are numbers describing position, and nothing in the labels says which one belongs to shells, so students attach the first number they meet to the first idea they meet.
misconceptions.correction: Read the electronic structure twice: 2,8,7 has three occupied shells, so Period 3, and seven outer electrons, so Group 7.

misconceptions.question: Are the elements in the modern table still placed in order of atomic weight?
misconceptions.correct: They are placed in order of atomic (proton) number.
misconceptions.misconception: The modern table is ordered by relative atomic mass, because that is the larger number printed in each box.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Relative atomic mass is printed on every data sheet and does usually rise from left to right, and it genuinely was the ordering rule in the earliest tables.
misconceptions.correction: Order is set by proton number, which rises by exactly one at each step. Where mass order disagrees, as with tellurium and iodine, proton number wins.

misconceptions.question: Which elements behave alike: those in the same row or those in the same column?
misconceptions.correct: Those in the same column, which is called a group.
misconceptions.misconception: Neighbours in the same row are the family of similar elements.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read the table left to right like text, so rows feel like the natural units, and a row does contain elements placed next to each other in the order.
misconceptions.correction: Similar properties run down the columns, because only elements in the same column share an outer-electron count.

misconceptions.question: Does periodic mean that the properties repeat exactly every eight elements?
misconceptions.correct: It means similar properties occur at regular intervals, not at a fixed interval of eight throughout.
misconceptions.misconception: Every eighth element is an exact repeat, all the way along the table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first two short periods do hold eight elements each, and Newlands' law of octaves is often taught alongside, so eight sticks in the memory as the rule.
misconceptions.correction: Later periods are longer, so the interval changes. The point is that the pattern returns regularly, which is what periodic means.

misconceptions.question: Could the elements be ordered by their number of neutrons?
misconceptions.correct: No. Order is by proton number, which is fixed for an element.
misconceptions.misconception: Neutron number sets the position, since neutrons sit in the nucleus too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Protons and neutrons are learned together as nuclear particles with almost equal mass, so they get treated as interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: Isotopes of one element have different neutron numbers but occupy a single place in the table, so neutrons cannot be setting the order.

misconceptions.question: Do all the elements in a group react at exactly the same rate?
misconceptions.correct: No. They react in similar ways, but reactivity changes steadily down the group.
misconceptions.misconception: Same group means identical behaviour, so lithium and potassium react with water equally fast.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students latch on to the phrase similar chemical properties and read similar as identical, and demonstrations often show only one member of a group.
misconceptions.correction: Similar means the same type of reaction. The vigour changes down the group: down Group 1 it rises, down Group 7 it falls.

misconceptions.question: Did Mendeleev arrange the elements in order of atomic number?
misconceptions.correct: No. He worked before protons were known and used atomic weights.
misconceptions.misconception: Mendeleev used atomic number, which is why his table looks like the modern one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: His table resembles the modern one closely, and students assume the resemblance must come from using the same rule rather than from a good approximation to it.
misconceptions.correction: Protons were not discovered until after Mendeleev's work. He ordered by atomic weight and then adjusted the order where the properties demanded it.

misconceptions.question: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his table?
misconceptions.correct: He thought elements that belonged in those places had not yet been discovered.
misconceptions.misconception: The gaps held elements he had found but could not classify.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A gap looks like a place where something has been taken out rather than a place reserved for something that has not yet arrived.
misconceptions.correction: The gaps were predictions. Elements with the properties he had predicted, such as germanium, were later discovered and filled them.

misconceptions.question: Were the early tables faulty because the atomic weights had been measured badly?
misconceptions.correct: No. The trouble was that strict weight order sometimes puts an element in a group it does not suit.
misconceptions.misconception: Better measurement of atomic weights would have fixed the early tables.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Blaming inaccurate apparatus is a familiar explanation for old science being wrong, and it avoids having to think about why the rule itself was flawed.
misconceptions.correction: Weight order fails because atomic weight depends on the mixture of isotopes, not on proton number. No improvement in measurement removes that.

misconceptions.question: Are isotopes different elements?
misconceptions.correct: No. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Each isotope is its own element and should have its own place in the table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Isotopes have different masses and different spoken names, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14, which makes them sound like separate substances.
misconceptions.correction: Element identity is set by proton number alone. All isotopes of an element share one place in the table and one set of chemical properties.

misconceptions.question: Did Mendeleev discover the elements that filled his gaps?
misconceptions.correct: No. He predicted their properties; other scientists later discovered them.
misconceptions.misconception: Mendeleev found the missing elements himself, which is why the gaps closed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: His name is attached to the whole story of the gaps, so the discoveries get attributed to him as well as the predictions.
misconceptions.correction: The strength of his work was the prediction. When others discovered elements matching his predicted properties, that evidence supported his table.

misconceptions.question: Do metals form negative ions?
misconceptions.correct: No. Elements that react to form positive ions are metals.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals form negative ions, because metals are the ones that react strongly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that metals react readily but not the direction of electron transfer, and negative is often the first ion charge met in a lesson on ions.
misconceptions.correction: Metals lose outer electrons, leaving more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive. Elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.

misconceptions.question: Where in the periodic table are the non-metals found?
misconceptions.correct: Towards the right and top of the table.
misconceptions.misconception: Non-metals sit on the left, where the small light elements are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hydrogen is a non-metal printed at the top left, so the whole left-hand side gets tagged as non-metal territory.
misconceptions.correction: Apart from hydrogen, the left and the bottom are metals. Non-metals form the block towards the right and top, including Groups 7 and 0.

misconceptions.question: Are most of the elements non-metals?
misconceptions.correct: No. The majority of elements are metals.
misconceptions.misconception: Non-metals are the majority, since the ones met in everyday chemistry are oxygen, carbon and nitrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The non-metals studied at GCSE are the common, familiar ones, so they feel numerous, while dozens of metals are never named in lessons.
misconceptions.correction: Count the table: the metal block, including the transition metals, takes up far more of it than the small non-metal region at the top right.

misconceptions.question: Does an atom become a positive ion by gaining protons?
misconceptions.correct: No. It loses electrons; the proton number never changes in a chemical reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: A 2+ charge means two protons have been added to the nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Positive charge is linked to protons, so becoming positive suggests gaining protons rather than losing electrons.
misconceptions.correction: Chemical reactions move only outer electrons. Magnesium, 2,8,2, loses its two outer electrons to become Mg2+, still with twelve protons.

misconceptions.question: Do metals lose all of their electrons when they react?
misconceptions.correct: No. They lose only the small number of electrons in the outer shell.
misconceptions.misconception: A metal atom empties itself of electrons, so magnesium could form Mg8+ or worse.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Losing electrons is remembered without any limit on how many, and inner shells are not pictured as being held more tightly.
misconceptions.correction: Only outer electrons take part. Metals lie on the left precisely because they have few outer electrons to lose, giving small charges such as 1+ and 2+.

misconceptions.question: Are the noble gases unreactive because their outer shells are empty?
misconceptions.correct: No. Their outer shells hold a stable arrangement, eight electrons or two for helium.
misconceptions.misconception: Group 0 means zero outer electrons, so there is nothing there to react with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The group is numbered 0 and other group numbers do give the outer-electron count, so the pattern is applied one step too far.
misconceptions.correction: Group 0 is the exception to that pattern. The outer shell is full, not empty, and a full shell is why no electrons are gained, lost or shared.

misconceptions.question: Does helium have eight outer electrons like the other noble gases?
misconceptions.correct: No. Helium has only two electrons, which fills its single shell.
misconceptions.misconception: All of the noble gases have eight outer electrons, without exception.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule of eight is stated so often that the one exception given alongside it does not stick in the memory.
misconceptions.correction: Helium has just one shell, and the first shell is full at two electrons. That is why helium is as unreactive as the rest of Group 0.

misconceptions.question: Do the boiling points of the noble gases fall going down Group 0?
misconceptions.correct: No. They increase with increasing relative atomic mass.
misconceptions.misconception: Heavier noble gas atoms boil at lower temperatures.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gases feel lighter and more volatile as a class, and the falling reactivity trend of Group 7 pulls the expectation in the wrong direction.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states plainly that boiling point increases with increasing relative atomic mass down the group: helium boils lowest, radon highest.

misconceptions.question: Do the noble gases exist as molecules made of two atoms?
misconceptions.correct: No. They do not easily form molecules at all and exist as single atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Like oxygen and chlorine, the noble gases go around in pairs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The common gases met first, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen and chlorine, are all diatomic, so being a gas gets linked to being a pair.
misconceptions.correction: A stable outer arrangement means there is nothing to gain from bonding, so noble gas atoms stay single.

misconceptions.question: How many electrons does a Group 1 atom have in its outer shell?
misconceptions.correct: One, which it loses when it reacts.
misconceptions.misconception: A Group 1 atom is one electron short of a full shell and gains seven when it reacts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both the number one and the idea of completing a shell are in play, and students who have just met Group 7 apply that reasoning to Group 1 unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: Group 1 atoms have one outer electron and lose it, forming a 1+ ion. Gaining seven would be far harder than losing one.

misconceptions.question: Does reactivity decrease going down Group 1?
misconceptions.correct: No. In Group 1 the reactivity of the elements increases going down the group.
misconceptions.misconception: Reactivity falls down every group, so lithium is the most reactive alkali metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Group 7 trend is often learned more firmly and then applied to Group 1, and lithium being at the top suggests that being first means being strongest.
misconceptions.correction: The two trends run opposite ways. Losing an electron gets easier down Group 1, so caesium reacts far more violently with water than lithium does.

misconceptions.question: Which gas is given off when sodium reacts with water?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen, together with sodium hydroxide solution.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxygen is released, because water contains oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The formula H2O contains oxygen, and the fizzing is assumed to be that oxygen escaping from the water.
misconceptions.correction: The metal takes the place of hydrogen: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2. The gas that pops with a lighted splint is hydrogen.

misconceptions.question: What is the formula of lithium oxide?
misconceptions.correct: Li2O, made from Li+ ions and O2- ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Lithium oxide is LiO, with one atom of each element.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Compound names give no ratio, so a one-to-one formula is the default guess whenever ionic charges are not checked.
misconceptions.correction: Lithium forms Li+ and oxygen forms O2-, so two lithium ions balance one oxide ion: 4Li + O2 → 2Li2O.

misconceptions.question: Do halogen atoms have one outer electron?
misconceptions.correct: No. They have seven outer electrons and gain one when they react.
misconceptions.misconception: Group 7 atoms have one outer electron, or else must lose seven in order to react.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number one is attached to the single electron gained, and the group number is then reused as the number that has to be lost.
misconceptions.correction: The group number is the outer-electron count, so Group 7 means seven. Gaining one completes the shell, which is far easier than losing seven.

misconceptions.question: What kind of compound forms when a halogen reacts with a metal?
misconceptions.correct: An ionic salt, such as sodium chloride.
misconceptions.misconception: Halogens always form molecules, so sodium chloride must be a molecule of shared electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Halogens are first met as diatomic molecules, so molecular bonding gets attached to the element itself rather than to the partner it reacts with.
misconceptions.correction: With a metal, electrons are transferred and an ionic salt forms. Only with a non-metal, as in hydrogen chloride, is the compound molecular.

misconceptions.question: Does reactivity increase going down Group 7?
misconceptions.correct: No. In Group 7 the reactivity of the elements decreases going down the group.
misconceptions.misconception: Iodine is more reactive than chlorine, because lower down the group means more reactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Group 1 trend is generalised to every group, and bigger atoms are assumed to be more powerful reactants.
misconceptions.correction: A halogen reacts by attracting an electron. Further down, the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the pull is weaker and reactivity falls.

misconceptions.question: Do the melting points of the halogens fall going down Group 7?
misconceptions.correct: No. Melting point and boiling point both rise going down the group.
misconceptions.misconception: Melting point falls down Group 7 because reactivity falls down Group 7.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two trends run down the same group in opposite directions, and students assume that every property must follow the reactivity trend.
misconceptions.correction: Physical trends and reactivity trends are separate. Down Group 7 relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point all increase, while reactivity decreases.

misconceptions.question: Can bromine displace chlorine from potassium chloride solution?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one.
misconceptions.misconception: Any halogen will displace any other halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word displacement is remembered as something that simply happens when the two are mixed, without the reactivity condition attached to it.
misconceptions.correction: Chlorine is above bromine, so chlorine displaces bromide: Cl2 + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br2. The reverse mixture gives no reaction.

misconceptions.question: Do the halogens exist as single atoms?
misconceptions.correct: No. They consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Chlorine gas is made of separate Cl atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The element is named and written in words as chlorine, and the subscript 2 in Cl2 is easily dropped when writing quickly.
misconceptions.correction: The halogens are diatomic: Cl2, Br2 and I2. Each atom shares one electron with the other so that both complete their outer shells.

misconceptions.question: In a halogen displacement reaction, is it the metal that gets displaced?
misconceptions.correct: No. One halogen takes the place of another; the metal stays in solution as its ion.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding chlorine to potassium bromide pushes out potassium metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Metal displacement reactions are taught using the same word, so the more familiar reaction is recalled in place of the halogen one.
misconceptions.correction: In Cl2 + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br2 the potassium ions are unchanged. The chlorine takes the bromide's place and bromine is set free, colouring the solution orange.

mcqs.stem: The modern periodic table sets the elements out one after another in order of which quantity?

options.text: Atomic (proton) number, which rises by exactly one from element to element
options.rationale: The specification states that elements are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number, and that number goes up by one at every step along the table.

options.text: Relative atomic mass, the quantity used by the very earliest tables
options.rationale: Relative atomic mass is printed in every box of the data sheet and usually does rise from left to right, and it really was the ordering rule before protons were known.

options.text: Number of outer-shell electrons, counted for each atom in turn
options.rationale: Students who know that outer electrons decide the groups assume they must also fix the overall order, but outer-electron counts repeat rather than climb.

options.text: Number of neutrons held in the nucleus of one atom
options.rationale: Protons and neutrons are learned together as nuclear particles, so they get treated as interchangeable, but isotopes share a place despite different neutron counts.

mcqs.stem: Why is the periodic table described as periodic?

options.text: Because similar properties turn up again at regular intervals
options.rationale: The specification gives exactly this reason: the table is called periodic because similar properties occur at regular intervals along the order of the elements.

options.text: Because the properties of the elements repeat exactly every eighth one
options.rationale: The first two short periods do hold eight elements, and Newlands' octaves are often taught nearby, so eight is remembered as a fixed rule rather than a special case.

options.text: Because each horizontal row of the table is called a period
options.rationale: The word period genuinely does label the rows, so the name looks self-explanatory, but this does not say why the arrangement works.

options.text: Because the table was revised at regular times as elements appeared
options.rationale: This reads periodic in its everyday sense of happening at intervals in time, which is the right idea applied to the wrong thing.

mcqs.stem: What do all the elements in one group of the periodic table share?

options.text: The same number of electrons in their outer shell
options.rationale: The specification states that elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, and that this gives them similar chemical properties.

options.text: The same number of occupied electron shells in the atom
options.rationale: This is what the period number tells you, and students who have swapped the two labels pick it confidently.

options.text: Almost the same relative atomic mass as one another
options.rationale: Mass is the most visible number in each box, and mass does rise steadily along a period, so it feels like the shared quantity.

options.text: The same total number of electrons in the whole atom
options.rationale: Equal electron totals would mean equal proton numbers, so these would all be the same element rather than a group of different ones.

mcqs.stem: Atom X has the electronic structure 2,8,2 and atom Y has 2,8,8,2. Why do X and Y have similar chemical properties?

options.text: Each has two electrons in its outer shell
options.rationale: Chemical properties are set by the outer electrons. Both structures end in 2, so both atoms are in Group 2 and react in the same way.

options.text: Each of them has an even number of electrons
options.rationale: An even total is a real pattern in these two structures but it has nothing to do with bonding, since only the outer shell takes part in reactions.

options.text: Each has the same number of filled inner shells
options.rationale: X has two inner shells and Y has three, so this is not even true, but students who count shells rather than outer electrons do not check.

options.text: Each sits in the same horizontal row of the table
options.rationale: X is in Period 3 and Y in Period 4, but students who think rows are the families reach for this without checking the shell count.

mcqs.stem: An atom of an element has the electronic structure 2,8,7. Where in the periodic table is this element?

options.text: Group 7 and Period 3, since it has seven outer electrons in three shells
options.rationale: The number of occupied shells gives the period and the outer-electron count gives the group, so 2,8,7 is in Period 3 and in Group 7.

options.text: Group 3 and Period 7, taking the two numbers the other way round
options.rationale: This is the commonest slip of all: the shell count is read as the group and the outer count as the period.

options.text: Group 2 and Period 3, using the first shell number for the group
options.rationale: Reading the group from the first figure in the list gives 2, which is a natural mistake for a student who works left to right.

options.text: Group 7 and Period 17, adding the seventeen electrons present
options.rationale: The total electron count, 17, is the proton number rather than the period, but it is a number the student has just worked out.

mcqs.stem: Rubidium lies directly below potassium in Group 1. What can be predicted about rubidium from its position?

options.text: It reacts with water even more vigorously than potassium does
options.rationale: Position in the table lets you predict probable reactivity. Reactivity increases going down Group 1, so rubidium reacts more vigorously than potassium.

options.text: It reacts with water far less vigorously than potassium
options.rationale: This applies the Group 7 trend to Group 1. The two groups run opposite ways, which is why the direction has to be recalled for each.

options.text: It reacts with water at just the same rate as potassium
options.rationale: Similar chemical properties is read as identical behaviour, so the steady change down the group is missed.

options.text: It forms a negative ion, unlike the metals above it
options.rationale: Rubidium is a metal and loses its single outer electron, but students who have not fixed the direction of electron transfer choose a negative charge.

mcqs.stem: Before protons, neutrons and electrons were discovered, scientists classified the elements by arranging them in order of what?

options.text: Their atomic weights, the one measured quantity they had
options.rationale: The specification states that before subatomic particles were known, scientists attempted to classify the elements by arranging them in order of their atomic weights.

options.text: Their atomic numbers, counted from the protons present
options.rationale: Mendeleev's table looks so like the modern one that students assume it must have used the modern rule, forgetting that protons were not yet known.

options.text: The number of electron shells that their atoms held
options.rationale: Shells are the explanation students meet first for periodicity, so they get projected back onto a time before electrons were discovered.

options.text: The order in which the elements had been discovered
options.rationale: Discovery order is a real historical sequence and sounds like something early chemists could have used, but it gives no chemical pattern.

mcqs.stem: What went wrong in early periodic tables when the strict order of atomic weights was followed?

options.text: Some elements were placed in groups that did not suit them
options.rationale: The specification states that early tables were incomplete and that strict atomic-weight order put some elements in inappropriate groups.

options.text: Every atomic weight had been measured far too inaccurately
options.rationale: Blaming the apparatus is a familiar way to explain old science being wrong, and it avoids questioning the ordering rule itself.

options.text: The elements had not been arranged into any columns at all
options.rationale: Early tables did have columns; what they lacked was a rule that put the right elements into them.

options.text: All of the tables listed the elements in rows, not columns
options.rationale: Rows and columns are easily swapped when recalling a diagram, and this sounds like a plausible structural fault.

mcqs.stem: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his periodic table?

options.text: He thought elements belonging in those places had not yet been found
options.rationale: The specification states that Mendeleev overcame some of the problems by leaving gaps for elements that he thought had not been discovered.

options.text: He had found elements that would not fit any of his groups
options.rationale: A gap looks like a place something was taken out of, rather than a place kept ready for something still to come.

options.text: He wanted to leave room for the isotopes of each element
options.rationale: Isotopes belong to the later part of this story, and students who meet the two ideas together often merge them.

options.text: He had discovered the elements and was saving their places
options.rationale: His name is attached to the whole episode, so the discoveries as well as the predictions get credited to him.

mcqs.stem: As well as leaving gaps, what else did Mendeleev do so that his groups worked?

options.text: He changed the order of some elements from strict weight order
options.rationale: The specification states that in some places Mendeleev changed the order based on atomic weights, so that elements fell into suitable groups.

options.text: He arranged every one of the elements by their atomic numbers
options.rationale: This is the modern rule read back into his work, but atomic number was not available to him.

options.text: He measured all of the atomic weights again to fix the order
options.rationale: Re-measuring sounds like the scientific response, but no measurement can repair a rule that is wrong in principle.

options.text: He took out of the table any element that spoiled a group
options.rationale: Deleting awkward data is the opposite of what he did, but it is a tempting way to imagine tidying up a table.

mcqs.stem: Knowledge of isotopes explained why atomic-weight order was not always correct. What is the explanation?

options.text: An element's atomic weight depends on the mixture of its isotopes
options.rationale: Because atomic weight is an average over isotopes, an element can have a larger weight than the element that follows it in proton order, as tellurium does before iodine.

options.text: Isotopes of an element are really separate elements in disguise
options.rationale: Different masses and names such as carbon-12 make isotopes sound like different substances needing their own places.

options.text: Isotopes give every atom of an element a different proton number
options.rationale: The particle that changes is the neutron, not the proton, but the two are easily swapped when both are described as nuclear.

options.text: Atomic weights slowly change over time as isotopes decay away
options.rationale: Radioactive decay is associated with isotopes, so a drifting weight sounds plausible to a student joining two half-remembered ideas.

mcqs.stem: Which statement identifies an element as a metal?

options.text: It reacts by forming positive ions
options.rationale: The specification defines metals in exactly this way: elements that react to form positive ions are metals.

options.text: It reacts by forming negative ions instead
options.rationale: Students remember that metals react readily but not which way the electrons go, and negative is often the first ion charge they meet.

options.text: It reacts by gaining additional protons
options.rationale: Positive charge is linked to protons, so gaining protons feels like the way for an atom to become positive.

options.text: It reacts by sharing its outer electrons
options.rationale: Sharing is the non-metal to non-metal route, and it is the bonding type most recently studied by many students.

mcqs.stem: Where in the periodic table are the non-metal elements found?

options.text: Towards the right-hand side and the top of the periodic table
options.rationale: The specification states that non-metals are found towards the right and top of the table, with metals to the left and towards the bottom.

options.text: Towards the left-hand side and the bottom of the table
options.rationale: Hydrogen is a non-metal printed at the top left, which tags the whole left side as non-metal territory for some students.

options.text: Spread fairly evenly across the whole of the table
options.rationale: If non-metals are believed to be the majority, they have to be spread everywhere for that belief to hold.

options.text: Only in the last column, which holds the noble gases
options.rationale: Group 0 is the most obviously non-metallic column, so it can be mistaken for the whole non-metal region.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of properties is typical of metals rather than of non-metals?

options.text: Good electrical conduction together with being malleable
options.rationale: Conducting electricity well and being malleable are characteristic physical properties of metals, and they follow from metallic structure and bonding.

options.text: Forming negative ions together with conducting poorly
options.rationale: Poor conduction is genuinely non-metallic, and pairing it with negative ions is exactly the error of reversing the direction of electron transfer.

options.text: Low melting points together with a dull and brittle surface
options.rationale: These are non-metal properties, chosen by students who recall a list of properties without recalling which column it belonged to.

options.text: Being gaseous at room temperature and having low density
options.rationale: Many non-metals are gases and most metals are dense solids, so this pairing is the wrong way round.

mcqs.stem: Why do the metals occupy the left-hand side of the periodic table?

options.text: Their atoms have few outer electrons, which are lost easily
options.rationale: Group number gives the outer-electron count, so the left-hand columns hold atoms with one, two or three outer electrons, which they lose to form positive ions.

options.text: Their atoms have many outer electrons, all lost quite easily
options.rationale: Losing electrons is remembered without the limit on how many, so having more of them is read as making an element more metallic.

options.text: Their atoms are the heaviest, so they are placed first
options.rationale: Position is confused with mass; in fact the heaviest atoms lie at the bottom of the table, not at the left.

options.text: Their atoms hold spare protons that give them a charge
options.rationale: Positive charge is again traced to protons rather than to electrons being removed.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium has the electronic structure 2,8,2. Which ion does it form when it reacts, and how?

options.text: Mg2+, by losing the two electrons in its outer shell
options.rationale: A metal reacts by losing its outer electrons. Magnesium loses two, leaving twelve protons and ten electrons, so the ion carries a 2+ charge.

options.text: Mg8+, by losing all the electrons in its second shell
options.rationale: Students who think a metal empties itself of electrons pick the inner shell count of eight.

options.text: Mg2-, by gaining two extra electrons into that outer shell
options.rationale: Completing the outer shell by gaining electrons is the non-metal route, applied here to a metal.

options.text: Mg2+, by gaining two more protons into its own nucleus
options.rationale: The charge is right but the mechanism is not; proton number cannot change in a chemical reaction.

mcqs.stem: Why are the noble gases in Group 0 unreactive?

options.text: Their atoms already have a stable arrangement of outer electrons
options.rationale: The specification states that the noble gases are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons.

options.text: Their atoms have no electrons at all in the outer shell
options.rationale: Group 0 is read as zero outer electrons, extending the group-number rule one step too far.

options.text: Their atoms are too heavy for the electrons to be moved
options.rationale: Helium is the lightest noble gas of all and is still unreactive, so mass cannot be the reason.

options.text: Their atoms are joined in pairs that use up the electrons
options.rationale: The first gases students meet are diatomic, so pairing gets attached to gases in general.

mcqs.stem: How many electrons are there in the outer shell of a helium atom?

options.text: Two, which is a full outer shell for helium
options.rationale: The specification notes helium as the exception: the noble gases have eight outer electrons, except helium, which has only two.

options.text: Eight, just the same as the other noble gases
options.rationale: The rule of eight is repeated so often that the exception stated beside it does not stick.

options.text: Zero, because helium has no outer shell
options.rationale: This follows from reading Group 0 as meaning no outer electrons at all.

options.text: Four, half of a completed outer shell
options.rationale: Halving eight is a tempting move for an atom described as smaller than the rest.

mcqs.stem: How do the boiling points of the noble gases change going down Group 0?

options.text: They increase as the relative atomic mass increases
options.rationale: The specification states that the boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass, that is, going down the group.

options.text: They stay the same, since all of these gases are unreactive
options.rationale: Unreactivity is treated as though it fixed every property, so no trend at all is expected.

options.text: They increase and then fall away lower down the group
options.rationale: A rise-then-fall pattern is a common guess when a student remembers there is a trend but not its shape.

options.text: They fall off as the relative atomic mass rises
options.rationale: Gases feel lighter and more volatile as a class, which pulls the expected trend the wrong way.

mcqs.stem: The boiling points of neon, argon and krypton are −246 °C, −186 °C and −153 °C. What is the best prediction for xenon?

options.text: About −108 °C, above krypton
options.rationale: Boiling point increases going down the group, so xenon, the next element down, must boil at a higher temperature than krypton's −153 °C.

options.text: About −280 °C, below all three
options.rationale: This continues the trend in the wrong direction, which is the standard error when the direction has not been fixed.

options.text: About −199 °C, midway between
options.rationale: Averaging the data given is a safe-looking move, but it places xenon inside the range rather than beyond it.

options.text: About −153 °C, the same as krypton
options.rationale: Same group is taken to mean identical properties, so no change is expected between neighbours.

mcqs.stem: Why do the Group 1 alkali metals all show the same characteristic properties?

options.text: Every one of their atoms has a single electron in its outer shell
options.rationale: The specification states that the Group 1 elements have characteristic properties because of the single electron in their outer shell.

options.text: Every one of their atoms is short of a single outer electron
options.rationale: Group 7 reasoning is carried over: the number one is remembered, but attached to a gap rather than to an electron present.

options.text: Every one of their atoms contains just one electron shell
options.rationale: Group is confused with period, so the one is read as a count of shells.

options.text: Every one of their atoms has the same atomic weight
options.rationale: Mass is the most visible number on the data sheet, so it gets offered as the shared quantity.

mcqs.stem: What is formed when sodium is dropped onto water?

options.text: Sodium hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas
options.rationale: An alkali metal reacts with water to give the metal hydroxide and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2.

options.text: Sodium hydroxide solution and oxygen gas as well
options.rationale: Water contains oxygen, so the fizzing is assumed to be oxygen escaping rather than hydrogen being displaced.

options.text: Sodium chloride solution and hydrogen
options.rationale: Sodium chloride is the sodium compound students know best, so it is offered even where no chlorine is present.

options.text: Sodium oxide powder and steam
options.rationale: The oxide is the product of burning sodium in air, and the two reactions of sodium are easily merged.

mcqs.stem: Lithium is burned in oxygen. Which equation describes the reaction correctly?

options.text: 4Li + O2 → 2Li2O, giving white lithium oxide
options.rationale: Lithium forms Li+ and oxygen forms O2-, so the oxide is Li2O, and four lithium atoms are needed to balance the two oxygen atoms in O2.

options.text: 4Li + O2 → 2Li2O, giving off hydrogen gas too
options.rationale: Hydrogen belongs to the reaction with water; students who have just met that reaction carry the gas across.

options.text: 2Li + O2 → 2LiO, giving white lithium oxide
options.rationale: A one-to-one formula is the default guess when ionic charges are not checked, and this equation does balance, which makes it look right.

options.text: Li + O2 → LiO2, white lithium oxide
options.rationale: Copying the subscript from O2 straight into the product is a very common way of writing an unbalanced formula.

mcqs.stem: Potassium is heated and lowered into a gas jar of chlorine. What is the product?

options.text: Potassium chloride, a white solid
options.rationale: An alkali metal burns in chlorine to give the metal chloride: 2K + Cl2 → 2KCl, a white ionic solid.

options.text: Potassium chloride, a green gaseous molecule
options.rationale: Chlorine's green colour and molecular nature are transferred to the compound, instead of an ionic solid being expected.

options.text: Potassium hydroxide, an alkaline solution
options.rationale: Hydroxide is the product of the reaction with water, and the three Group 1 reactions are easily mixed up.

options.text: Potassium chlorate, a colourless liquid
options.rationale: Chlorate is a real chlorine-containing name that students have seen, and it is chosen when chloride and chlorate are not distinguished.

mcqs.stem: Why does reactivity increase going down Group 1?

options.text: The outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily
options.rationale: Each element down the group has another occupied shell, so the single outer electron is further out and less strongly held, and is therefore lost more readily.

options.text: The outer electron is held closer to the nucleus further down
options.rationale: Getting the geometry backwards produces the opposite trend, which is why some students state the Group 7 direction here.

options.text: The atoms gain more outer electrons as the group is descended
options.rationale: The outer-electron count is constant down a group; it is the number of shells that changes.

options.text: The atoms hold more protons, so they pull electrons in harder
options.rationale: Proton number does rise down the group, so this is a genuine piece of reasoning, but it ignores the extra shells in between.

mcqs.stem: Caesium lies below rubidium in Group 1. A small piece is dropped into water. What is the best prediction?

options.text: It reacts explosively, faster than rubidium does
options.rationale: Reactivity increases going down Group 1, so caesium, which is below rubidium, reacts even more violently than rubidium with water.

options.text: It reacts slowly, more slowly than lithium does
options.rationale: This is the Group 7 trend applied to Group 1, which puts the least reactive metal at the bottom.

options.text: It reacts at just the same speed as rubidium
options.rationale: Similar properties within a group is read as identical properties, so no change is predicted.

options.text: It does not react, being a very heavy metal
options.rationale: Heavy metals such as gold are famously unreactive, so weight is taken as a sign of stability.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the halogens in Group 7 is correct?

options.text: They have seven outer electrons and form diatomic molecules
options.rationale: The specification states that the halogens have seven electrons in their outer shell, are non-metals, and consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms.

options.text: They have just one outer electron and form molecules of two atoms
options.rationale: The single electron gained in reactions is misremembered as the number present in the outer shell.

options.text: They have seven outer electrons and exist as single atoms only
options.rationale: The subscript 2 in Cl2 is easily dropped, and the element is named in words as chlorine rather than as a pair.

options.text: They are metals holding seven electrons in the outer shell
options.rationale: Elements that react vigorously are assumed to be metals, and the halogens are met through their vigorous reactions.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine reacts with sodium. What sort of compound is produced?

options.text: An ionic compound, sodium chloride
options.rationale: A halogen reacting with a metal gains an electron from it, so the product is an ionic salt, here sodium chloride.

options.text: A molecule of shared electron pairs
options.rationale: Halogens are first met as diatomic molecules, so molecular bonding is attached to the halogen itself.

options.text: A mixture of sodium and chlorine atoms
options.rationale: Mixture and compound are confused by students who do not see that a chemical change has taken place.

options.text: An alloy of the metal with chlorine
options.rationale: Alloy is the word for a metal combination, and it is reached for whenever a metal is one of the reactants.

mcqs.stem: Which compound forms when chlorine reacts with the non-metal hydrogen?

options.text: Hydrogen chloride, a molecular compound with a shared pair of electrons
options.rationale: Two non-metals react by sharing electrons, so chlorine and hydrogen give the molecular compound hydrogen chloride, HCl.

options.text: Hydrogen chloride, an ionic compound built from hydrogen ions
options.rationale: Hydrogen chloride does form ions when it dissolves in water, so the compound itself gets labelled ionic.

options.text: Hydrogen chlorate, a molecular compound of three elements
options.rationale: Chlorate is a familiar-sounding name, and it is chosen when chloride and chlorate are not told apart.

options.text: Chlorine hydride, an ionic salt of the metal hydrogen
options.rationale: Hydrogen sits at the top left of the table, which leads some students to treat it as a metal forming a salt.

mcqs.stem: The melting points of chlorine, bromine and iodine are −101 °C, −7 °C and 114 °C. What is the best prediction for astatine?

options.text: Above 114 °C, since melting point rises down the group
options.rationale: Melting point increases going down Group 7, so astatine, which lies below iodine, must melt above iodine's 114 °C.

options.text: Below −101 °C, since melting point falls down the group
options.rationale: The reactivity trend does fall down Group 7, and it is assumed that every property must follow it.

options.text: Around 54 °C, between the bromine and iodine values
options.rationale: Averaging the figures given looks cautious, but it places astatine inside the range instead of beyond it.

options.text: Exactly 114 °C, the same as iodine above it
options.rationale: Same group is again read as identical properties rather than as a steady trend.

mcqs.stem: Why does the reactivity of the halogens decrease going down Group 7?

options.text: The outer shell is further out, so an electron is attracted less
options.rationale: A halogen reacts by gaining one electron. Further down the group the outer shell is further from the nucleus with more shells in between, so the attraction is weaker.

options.text: The atoms have to lose seven electrons, which gets harder lower down
options.rationale: The group number is read as the number of electrons that must be lost, rather than the number already present.

options.text: The outer shell moves closer to the nucleus further down the group
options.rationale: Getting the geometry backwards is the usual route to stating the Group 1 direction for Group 7.

options.text: The atoms are heavier, so they move more slowly
options.rationale: Heavier particles do move more slowly, so this is real physics applied to the wrong property.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine solution is added to potassium bromide solution. What happens?

options.text: Bromine is displaced and the solution turns orange
options.rationale: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromide from solution: Cl2 + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br2, and the free bromine colours the solution orange.

options.text: Chlorine is displaced by the bromide and a green gas forms
options.rationale: Displacement is remembered as something that simply happens on mixing, without the condition that the added halogen must be the more reactive one.

options.text: Potassium is displaced and floats about on the surface
options.rationale: Metal displacement uses the same word, so the more familiar reaction is recalled in its place.

options.text: No reaction happens, as chlorine is below bromine
options.rationale: This depends on the reversed Group 7 order, in which iodine would be the most reactive halogen.
